doc.title: Peter Vacher interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001

title: British players who moved to the United States
summary: British players felt pride when Shearing, Ronnie Ball and Victor Feldman succeeded in America; Keith Ingham should not be blamed.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: I don’t know how to ask this question, but do British people resent the fact that a lot of your best artists seem to come here and stay?

Well originally I think we felt great pride you see. The idea was that if you could make it in the States, by golly that was a tremendous accolade. Because after all America was the home of the music. So when let’s say someone like Shearing came here, Ronnie Ball, the bebop piano player, came here, of course Victor Feldman.

One of our great exports. There was a sense, it’s a kind of coals to Newcastle thing. Hey, if these guys have been able to make it in the States, which is the home of the music, that’s a tremendous plaudit for them. And I think that was the attitude that most of us took. I don’t think there’s an opinion now. No one would say of Keith Ingham my gosh he sold out by going to the States, he should have stayed home. That’s fair enough. Today’s environment, why shouldn’t he go here. Let him go where he wants to go, let him see what he can do you know.
